children.title: DOJ Files Judicial-Misconduct Complaint Against Judge James Boasberg
children.description_short: The Justice Department filed a misconduct complaint against Judge Boasberg on July 29, 2025; the Sixth Circuit dismissed it in December.
children.description_medium: On July 29, 2025, the Justice Department filed a judicial-misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg with the D.C. Circuit’s Judicial Council. The complaint alleged misconduct based on remarks at a March Judicial Conference and Boasberg’s handling of litigation over removals under the Alien Enemies Act. A Sixth Circuit order later dismissed it, citing insufficient evidence and other Rule 11 grounds; the allegations were not findings against Boasberg.
children.description_long: On July 29, 2025, the Justice Department filed a judicial-misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg with the D.C. Circuit’s Judicial Council. The complaint alleged that comments Boasberg reportedly made during a March Judicial Conference and his rulings in litigation over removals under the Alien Enemies Act violated judicial ethics canons. Those statements were allegations in the complaint, not findings. After the proceeding was transferred to the Sixth Circuit, Chief Judge Jeffrey Sutton dismissed it on December 19, 2025. The order said the complaint lacked sufficient evidence and was related in part to the merits of rulings; it also noted that DOJ had not supplied an attachment it cited as evidence. The order resolved the misconduct complaint, not the separate underlying deportation litigation. Reuters reported the filing on July 28, while the Sixth Circuit order gives July 29 as the filing date; this card uses the court’s date. The complaint’s dismissal is stated without implying that Boasberg committed misconduct or that the underlying litigation ended on that date.

children.title: Trump Administration Makes 34 Emergency Requests to the Supreme Court by March 2026
children.description_short: A Brennan Center tally says the administration sought emergency Supreme Court intervention 34 times by March 2026; 25 requests had decisions, with an 80% win rate.
children.description_medium: A Brennan Center tally published April 28, 2026, reported that by March the second Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court to intervene 34 times when lower courts blocked parts of its agenda. The Court had issued 25 shadow-docket decisions on those requests and ruled for the administration in 80 percent of them. These are the Center’s counts; they do not establish that each request produced a final merits judgment or a lasting policy change.
children.description_long: By March 2026, the second Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court to intervene 34 times after lower courts blocked parts of its agenda, according to a Brennan Center for Justice tally published April 28, 2026. The Center reported that the Court issued 25 shadow-docket decisions on those requests and ruled for the administration in 80 percent of them. This is a count of emergency requests and resulting decisions, not a count of final merits judgments or proof that every requested policy became permanent. The reported win rate has 25 decisions as its denominator; the source does not claim that all 34 requests received decisions by that date. Because this record combines separate matters from the Boasberg complaint, it treats the tally as a distinct administration-wide pattern over time. The applications’ use of an established emergency process does not alone show misconduct, and the count does not supply individual case outcomes or quantified harms. It is attributed to the Brennan Center, whose policy article advances reforms to Supreme Court practice. The card therefore records its measure and scope without presenting the Center’s characterization of the docket as a court finding.

title: 1993 Mar-a-Lago Use Agreement Prohibited Membership Discrimination
description_short: A 1993 Palm Beach agreement governing Mar-a-Lago's club use barred discrimination against prospective members on listed grounds.
description_medium: On August 10, 1993, Donald Trump, Mar-a-Lago Club, Inc., and the Town of Palm Beach entered a Declaration of Use Agreement governing the property’s private-club use. The agreement prohibited discrimination against prospective members on enumerated grounds, including race and religion. The document supports a 1993 membership rule; it does not establish a 2013 discrimination lawsuit or settlement, or prove how the rule was enforced.
description_long: On August 10, 1993, Donald J. Trump, the Town of Palm Beach, and The Mar-a-Lago Club, Inc. entered a Declaration of Use Agreement as the property was approved for use as a private social club. The recorded agreement says the Club “shall not discriminate against any prospective member” on listed grounds that include race, color, and religion. It set a nondiscrimination condition for prospective club membership. The document does not report a finding that Mar-a-Lago had discriminated, identify a plaintiff harmed by discrimination, or describe a 2013 lawsuit. PolitiFact’s review of a related but distinct Palm Beach dispute says Trump sued the town in 1996, alleging the town discriminated against Mar-a-Lago because it admitted Jewish and African American members; the town disputed that allegation. That was a claim by Trump against the town, not a case against the club brought by residents. This entry replaces the unsupported 2013-settlement story with the specific contractual clause established by the 1993 agreement. It does not infer whether the clause was enforced or whether it changed the club’s actual membership practices.

disposition: Corrected to Trump's documented June 4, 2018 public statement that he had an absolute right to pardon himself. The sources do not show that he issued a pardon or made this claim on January 20, 2025.
title: Trump Claims an “Absolute Right” to Pardon Himself
description_short: In a June 4, 2018 tweet, Trump claimed an absolute right to pardon himself during the Mueller investigation; he did not issue a self-pardon.
description_medium: On June 4, 2018, President Donald Trump tweeted that he had the “absolute right” to pardon himself while discussing the special counsel’s Russia investigation. He said he would not do so because he had done nothing wrong. This was a claim about presidential authority, not an issued pardon; the cited reporting describes the constitutional question as disputed.
description_long: On June 4, 2018, while Robert Mueller’s investigation was underway, President Donald Trump publicly claimed that he had an “absolute right” to pardon himself. In the same tweet, he said he had done nothing wrong and asked why he would use such a pardon. Associated Press coverage described the statement as asserting presidential power during the administration’s legal defense against the Russia investigation. Trump did not issue a self-pardon in the reported statement, and the sources do not show an order purporting to pardon him. The claim concerned whether a president could exercise the constitutional pardon power over himself; the question was disputed and no court ruling in this record resolves it. This corrected card dates the statement to June 2018. It does not attribute a self-pardon announcement to Trump’s return to office in January 2025, and it does not say that the Supreme Court’s 2024 presidential-immunity ruling conferred a pardon power. It records the public assertion and preserves the difference between an argument about authority and an act using that authority.

impact_proposal.confidence_reason: Reporting confirms the statement, while the impact estimate concerns a public legal claim rather than an issued pardon.
impact_proposal.rationale: The verified event is a president's public claim of self-pardon authority during an active federal investigation. No pardon was issued in the cited account, so this proposal scores no realized harm or private benefit and only limited institutional pressure.
impact_proposal.basis: Trump's June 4, 2018 tweet stated he had an absolute right to pardon himself; coverage described the issue as disputed.
impact_proposal.notes: Editorial comparative estimate under impact-v2, not a criminal or constitutional finding.

disposition: Replaced the unsupported claim of an all-program February rollback with a documented, narrower action: temporary withholding notices for 22 Title X grants issued March 31, effective April 1, 2025. The broader ACA-repeal and all-support claims remain unverified.
title: Administration Temporarily Withholds 22 Title X Grants
description_short: On March 31, 2025, Title X grantees were notified that the administration would temporarily withhold funding for 22 grants beginning April 1.
description_medium: On March 31, 2025, 16 Title X grantees received notices that the Trump administration was temporarily withholding funds for 22 fiscal year 2025 grants, effective April 1. Title X supports family-planning care, including contraception. The Guttmacher Institute estimated that if the withholding became permanent, at least 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care over a year; that figure is conditional, not a count of confirmed losses.
description_long: On March 31, 2025, 16 Title X grantees received notices that the Trump administration was temporarily withholding funding from 22 fiscal year 2025 grants, effective April 1. Title X supports family-planning services, including contraception, for low-income people. The Guttmacher Institute reported that all 13 direct grants to Planned Parenthood affiliates were included among the 22. It estimated that, if the withholding became permanent, at least 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care in a year. That estimate is conditional: it is not a count of people already deprived of care. The evidence supports a temporary, targeted withholding in April 2025. This card does not repeat the original assertions that all federal contraceptive support ended in February or that the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive coverage requirement was rescinded then; the cited record establishes the Title X grant action. The estimate and consequences remain attributed to Guttmacher, and the sources reviewed do not establish whether the withheld funds were later restored or how many patients lost services.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

impact_proposal.confidence_reason: The notices and temporary funding action are documented; the largest cited access effect is a conditional estimate if withholding became permanent.
impact_proposal.rationale: The administration temporarily withheld funding for a portion of Title X grants, a program that supports family planning and contraception. The potential access loss is serious but remains conditional, so the estimate is not counted as realized harm; no evidence here establishes institutional damage, procedural abuse, or private gain.
impact_proposal.basis: Sixteen grantees were notified of temporary withholding for 22 FY2025 grants effective April 1; Guttmacher estimated potential effects if the withholding became permanent.
impact_proposal.notes: Editorial estimate under impact-v2, not measured patient harm.
